sections.heading: The sequence beyond its best-known poems
paragraphs: The book opens with the dialogue Michael Robartes and the Dancer, followed by Solomon and the Witch, An Image from a Past Life and Under Saturn. A concentrated group of political poems follows: Easter, 1916, Sixteen Dead Men, The Rose Tree, On a Political Prisoner and The Leaders of the Crowd. Towards Break of Day and Demon and Beast precede The Second Coming. The closing three poems are A Prayer for My Daughter, A Meditation in Time of War and To be Carved on a Stone at Bally-Lee, the title used in the Cuala printing.

This order matters when reading the volume as a collection. Dialogues about love and knowledge stand beside arguments about political commitment; the final inscription names Yeats, his wife George, the materials used to repair their tower and the local forge. The book ends with a particular building and a wish for its inscription to survive the building’s eventual ruin.

sections.heading: Political remembrance and its qualifications
paragraphs: Easter, 1916 records a change in Yeats’s judgement of people he had previously encountered in ordinary social life. Its final stanza names MacDonagh, MacBride, Connolly and Pearse, but remembrance does not settle the poem’s questions about sacrifice, prolonged commitment or the necessity of the deaths. The movement between acknowledgement and doubt is present in the wording of the poem itself.

The neighbouring poems approach political death through different forms. Sixteen Dead Men addresses an unnamed opponent in a short argument about the dead and the living. The Rose Tree gives Pearse and Connolly a dialogue about a tree deprived of water. Keeping these poems together makes it possible to compare the claims made by individual speakers with the more openly questioning account in Easter, 1916.

sections.heading: A book made by the Cuala Press
paragraphs: Cuala belonged to the printing and craft enterprise established by the Yeats sisters after their separation from Dun Emer in 1908. Elizabeth Corbet Yeats managed the press, while Susan Mary, known as Lily, directed the embroidery work. The publication therefore belongs to the history of Irish women’s printing and publishing as well as to W. B. Yeats’s bibliography.

Yeats’s own Preface acknowledges that his philosophical references may need explanation. It introduces the purported exposition of Geraldus by Michael Robartes and directs readers towards two notes. Those notes form part of the original book’s presentation of the poems; they are distinct from the later Astor annotations. The Preface also describes the time required to set, print and dry a hand-printed book, providing a contemporary account of the production process behind this small collection.

sections.heading: How the narrator obtains his account
paragraphs: The visiting engineer first notices Ethan at the post office. Harmon Gow supplies information about the accident and the Frome family, while the narrator’s landlady, Mrs Ned Hale, knows a different part of the history. An interruption to the narrator’s usual transport arrangements brings him into Ethan’s sleigh; a snowstorm eventually takes him into the Frome kitchen. The story’s opening is therefore an account of how access to a household is acquired.

Wharton places a substantial reconstructed narrative between the engineer’s first-person opening and his return at the end. The central chapters describe Ethan’s private thoughts with a fullness the engineer’s conversations cannot independently establish. Readers can distinguish what the visitors and villagers directly report from what the framing narrator arranges into a continuous account. That distinction is especially useful when considering the judgements made about Zeena.

sections.heading: Two evenings and a broken dish
paragraphs: The early chapters give unusually close attention to ordinary domestic arrangements. Ethan walks Mattie home after a village dance, notices who might court her and imagines the kitchen they will enter. When Zeena travels to Bettsbridge for medical advice, Ethan and Mattie have an evening alone. The meal, the position of a chair and the work of washing dishes become occasions for Ethan to imagine a married life they do not have.

Mattie has used a red glass pickle-dish that Zeena keeps among her valued possessions. The cat knocks it down, and Ethan attempts to conceal the breakage until he can obtain glue. Zeena’s discovery connects a household object with the argument over Mattie’s place in the home. The dish has a known history as a wedding present, so its importance comes from ownership, marriage and the rules of the household as well as from its colour.

sections.heading: Credit, wages and the cost of leaving
paragraphs: The obstacles to departure are set out in specific transactions. Andrew Hale normally pays for Ethan’s lumber after three months; Ethan’s request for a fifty-dollar advance is unusual and unsuccessful. Hale is himself short of money while preparing a house for his son’s marriage. Later, Ethan considers obtaining the advance by appealing to the Hales’ sympathy for Zeena’s illness, then abandons the plan when Mrs Hale speaks kindly about his care for his wife.

Mattie’s position is equally insecure. Her earlier attempts at paid work have damaged her health, and dismissal would send her away without a reliable means of support. Zeena’s proposal to employ a hired girl makes household labour an immediate financial question. These details explain why Ethan’s thoughts about running away repeatedly return to money, available work and the consequences for people left behind.

sections.heading: What changed between the early books
paragraphs: The short Advertisement to the 1798 volume describes most of its poems as experiments in the use of conversational language. It asks readers to judge their treatment of people, incidents and feeling without relying entirely on established expectations about poetic style. This is a different document from the substantial Preface associated with the two-volume edition of 1800.

The physical history of the first edition also records a late change. The National Library of New Zealand’s copy identifies replacement leaves through which Coleridge’s Lewti was removed and The Nightingale inserted, with a corrected contents leaf. Such evidence shows that the contents and appearance of the book were decisions made during publication. The Astor selection should be read according to its stated 1798 and 1800 sources, rather than treated as a later collected edition of either poet.

sections.heading: Speakers who disagree about an event
paragraphs: In We Are Seven, an adult questioner and a child cannot agree on how to count a family that includes two dead children. The disagreement persists to the final stanza. The poem supplies the child’s account of visiting the graves and the adult’s repeated arithmetic, allowing the exchange itself to carry the argument.

The Thorn presents a different problem of testimony. Its speaker repeatedly describes a tree, a mound and Martha Ray, but relies on local reports when explaining what may have happened to her child. Statements of certainty coexist with admissions of ignorance. These poems give readers practical reasons to ask who is speaking, what that speaker has seen and which conclusions belong to other people.

sections.heading: The early Mariner and the rural poems
paragraphs: The 1798 Ancyent Marinere begins the original volume with a wedding guest detained by a stranger’s story. Its archaic spelling and supernatural voyage differ markedly from the ordinary conversations elsewhere in the book. It also predates the marginal prose gloss Coleridge added in 1817. Reading the early poem keeps those two stages of its textual history separate.

The 1800 volume extends the range of rural narratives. In Michael, a shepherd’s financial obligation leads him to send his son Luke away, while an unfinished sheepfold preserves a visible trace of their agreement. Nutting recounts the speaker’s destruction of a woodland enclosure and his later response to it. These works place work, property, memory and responsibility within particular actions and places. They reward attention to the circumstances of each poem rather than a single general description of Romantic writing as the appreciation of scenery.

sections.heading: Salvage, tools and repeated experiments
paragraphs: Crusoe’s survival begins with repeated trips to the wreck, from which he obtains food, weapons, ammunition, tools, clothing and materials. His island work consequently depends on manufactured objects carried by the ship. A saw, an axe, nails and gunpowder make possible activities he could not easily begin with what the island alone provides.

The narrative records unsuccessful work as well as useful inventions. Crusoe makes a large canoe before discovering that he cannot move it to the water. Growing grain involves learning the seasons and preserving seed after mistakes; making earthenware requires repeated attempts and an accidental discovery about firing clay. The time spent describing these processes distinguishes the complete novel from abridgements that chiefly retain the footprint, Friday and the mutiny.

sections.heading: A journal inside a remembered life
paragraphs: The island story is told twice at different levels. Crusoe first recounts the wreck and his preparations retrospectively, then inserts a dated journal that returns to his arrival on 30 September 1659. The journal records weather, labour, illness and supplies. Its limits are material: the keeping of written records depends on the ink and paper he has salvaged.

The retrospective narrator also reviews his earlier explanations of events. When grain appears near his dwelling, he initially interprets it as a miracle and subsequently remembers shaking out a bag that had contained grain. During illness, dreams and biblical reading alter the way he understands his circumstances. Tracking these corrections makes the religious argument more precise: the book repeatedly distinguishes an event, Crusoe’s first interpretation and the account he gives after further thought.

sections.heading: Commerce before and after the island
paragraphs: The Brazilian plantation is part of the novel’s financial structure throughout. Crusoe leaves it to join an expedition seeking enslaved people, and after his return to Europe he discovers that his interests in Brazil have accumulated substantial value. His eventual wealth does not come simply from the crops and livestock he develops on the island. It also depends on property, trade and the work conducted in his absence.

Friday is preceded by Xury, the boy who escapes captivity with Crusoe on the African coast. Crusoe later transfers Xury to the Portuguese captain under an arrangement that includes a promise of freedom after ten years if he becomes Christian. Remembering this earlier relationship helps readers follow the distinctions Crusoe makes between friendship, service, religious conversion and ownership. The complete narrative also continues after the island rescue, including the return through Europe and an overland encounter with wolves; the familiar castaway story is one large part of a longer life account.

sections.heading: What Murry could establish about the collection
paragraphs: John Middleton Murry’s introductory note makes an important distinction: Mansfield had chosen the title The Doves’ Nest and Other Stories, but he could not say that she would have selected exactly the contents he published. He printed a plan dated 27 October 1921 that marked proposed stories as London or New Zealand pieces. The item provisionally called At Karori became The Doll’s House.

Murry also describes the surviving documents. For the title story he found a clean typescript but no further manuscript; Weak Heart survived as an opening, notes from the middle and a rapidly written ending. These details explain why a posthumous collection cannot automatically be treated as a volume the author completed and approved. The Astor selection preserves that distinction by identifying its four unfinished works.

sections.heading: Social position in the completed stories
paragraphs: The Doll’s House follows the Burnell children as they display a new toy to selected schoolfellows. Lil and Else Kelvey are excluded because of their family’s social position; their mother works as a washerwoman, and their father is the subject of hostile rumours. Kezia’s invitation briefly crosses a boundary enforced by adults as well as children. The small lamp inside the house becomes a particular object shared by Kezia’s attention and Else’s memory.

A Cup of Tea transfers questions of access and generosity to an affluent woman’s home. Rosemary Fell brings a poor young woman indoors after being asked for money, but her response changes when her husband comments on the visitor’s appearance. Honeymoon and Taking the Veil are different in scale: each concentrates on a young woman’s imaginative response to an immediate experience, allowing thought to move beyond what another person in the scene understands.

sections.heading: Grief, memory and interrupted narration
paragraphs: In The Fly, an office visit introduces the subject of two sons killed in the war. After the visitor leaves, the boss attempts to recover his grief, then turns his attention to a fly struggling in ink. The story’s final failure of recollection is part of its action; Mansfield does not provide an explanation that resolves the relation between the remembered son and the treatment of the insect.

The Canary takes the form of a woman’s account of a dead bird that had kept her company during domestic work. Six Years After, an unfinished piece, brings bereavement into a husband and wife’s journey by steamer. Read together, these works offer different narrative circumstances for remembering a loss: conversation in an office, direct address to a listener and thought during travel. Their differences remain important, including the distinction between a deliberately completed ending and the point at which a surviving fragment stops.

sections.heading: The dates and the missing replies
paragraphs: The dated narrative opens on 4 May 1771 and runs into December 1772. Its first book records Werther’s arrival in the countryside and his growing attachment to Charlotte; the second includes his employment away from her and his return. The intervals between letters are part of the construction. A change of date can move the reader over developments that Werther has not described as they occurred.

Most letters are addressed to Wilhelm, but Wilhelm’s replies are not printed as an equal, alternating correspondence. Readers encounter his advice when Werther answers or resists it. Charlotte and Albert likewise appear mainly through Werther’s reports until the fictional editor supplies a different account near the end. The editor’s intervention does not turn the preceding letters into a neutral record: it makes their omissions and the limits of Werther’s access to other minds more evident.

sections.heading: Employment and the restrictions of rank
paragraphs: Werther’s experience in official employment occupies a substantial part of the second book. He quarrels with his superior over administrative routine and writing style, while valuing the friendship of Count C. Personal ability and sympathy do not free him from the distinctions maintained by aristocratic society.

At the count’s house, Werther remains as titled guests assemble and is made to understand that his presence is unwelcome. The humiliation becomes a public story discussed by others. This episode gives his distress a social setting beyond the relationship with Charlotte: the same narrator who seeks intimacy and recognition also encounters rules about who may enter a room and remain there. His subsequent resignation should be read alongside those restrictions rather than reduced to an unexplained failure to settle into work.

sections.heading: Books within Werther’s letters
paragraphs: Werther describes reading Homer in the early countryside letters, linking the poems with ordinary domestic scenes and the work of preparing food. Later, the poetry attributed to Ossian becomes increasingly important. These references identify what the character reads and the language through which he describes his own circumstances.

During a late meeting, Charlotte asks Werther to read his translation of Ossian. The long passage interrupts the immediate story with accounts of separated lovers, storms and death; the listeners then identify their own situation with what they have heard. Literature is therefore an action within the plot as well as a subject for annotation. The passage records Werther and Charlotte’s response to a text, which is different from treating the inserted poems as a direct statement of Goethe’s judgement on their relationship.

sections.heading: A day shared by several different Londons
paragraphs: The novel repeatedly allows a public incident to connect people who do not know one another. A motor car draws speculation from a crowd; an aeroplane writes an advertisement in the sky; clocks and passing traffic are heard from different positions. Woolf can move between observers while keeping the shared incident in view. The resulting account includes private memories that the other people present cannot hear.

The city is also geographically and socially divided. Clarissa’s flower-buying, Peter Walsh’s walk, Septimus and Rezia’s time in Regent’s Park, and Elizabeth Dalloway’s excursion towards the Strand take place in different circumstances. Elizabeth’s thoughts about a possible profession differ from Miss Kilman’s dependence and resentment. Following these journeys helps distinguish a character’s recollections from events taking place elsewhere during the same day.

sections.heading: The people who remember Bourton
paragraphs: Bourton, the country house of Clarissa’s youth, enters the novel through memories revisited by people who have since led separate lives. Clarissa recalls Sally Seton and her rejection of Peter’s marriage proposal. Peter returns from India with his own interpretation of those events. When Sally arrives at the party as Lady Rosseter, her present circumstances complicate the image retained from youth.

The novel does not appoint one of these recollections as a complete account of the past. Small gestures and remembered conversations acquire different importance for different people. Richard’s attempt to express his affection by bringing Clarissa flowers is another example of the distance between intention and speech: the reader knows more of his preparation than Clarissa is told. Attending to such differences makes the transitions between viewpoints easier to follow.

sections.heading: Institutions, advice and public influence
paragraphs: Lady Bruton’s luncheon provides a concrete instance of political influence conducted through private sociability. Richard Dalloway and Hugh Whitbread help her prepare a letter to The Times concerning emigration to Canada. The scene shows the labour behind a public intervention, including the value assigned to Hugh’s command of the appropriate style.

Septimus encounters institutional authority in a different form. Dr Holmes repeatedly minimises his condition; Sir William Bradshaw prescribes separation and rest, exercising power through the language of professional judgement. Rezia’s observations and her attempts to protect time alone with her husband provide another account of his needs. The hat-making scene briefly records their practical cooperation before medical intervention returns. When the Bradshaws carry news of his death into the party, a private crisis enters Clarissa’s social world through the very people associated with his treatment.

sources.label: Virginia Woolf: Mrs Dalloway, complete text

sections.heading: How the essay makes its case
paragraphs: The opening does not immediately present a list of conclusions. Woolf constructs a narrator who walks, eats, reads, encounters restrictions and records the thoughts these experiences provoke. The contrast between an elaborate college luncheon and a plain dinner at Fernham gives institutional wealth a concrete form. The attempt to enter a library then makes permission and membership part of the act of research.

At the British Museum, the narrator finds abundant writing about women but struggles to obtain the sort of knowledge she needs. She begins to question the interests and emotions of the people who produced those books. The essay consequently examines evidence as well as exclusion: a large quantity of printed material about a group does not necessarily preserve that group’s experience or provide an impartial account of it.

sections.heading: Invented writers and an imagined literary future
paragraphs: Judith Shakespeare is one of several deliberately invented figures. Later, Woolf introduces Mary Carmichael and her supposed novel Life’s Adventure. The narrator considers its broken expectations of sentence and sequence before reaching Chloe and Olivia, two women who share a laboratory. The example asks what happens when fictional women have work and relationships that cannot be described only through their connection to men.

These passages are thought experiments within Woolf’s argument, not recovered biographies or reviews of an identifiable historical book. The distinction matters when using the essay as a source. Its discussion of actual writers such as Aphra Behn and Jane Austen operates beside constructed cases designed to expose what existing literary records have left unrepresented. The movement between those methods is part of the book’s form.

sections.heading: Income, privacy and the inherited sentence
paragraphs: The narrator explains that a legacy from an aunt has given her five hundred pounds a year. She contrasts the security of that income with work done under pressure and with the need to please people who control employment. The sum has a stated practical function in the argument: it secures time and independence from particular patrons or employers. Woolf does not offer it as a modern budget that can be transferred unchanged between periods.

The essay also asks what a woman inherits when she begins to write. Woolf considers Austen’s ability to work in a common sitting-room, Charlotte Brontë’s interruptions of narrative by argument, and the fitness of available prose forms for a writer’s experience. These are Woolf’s critical judgements, open to examination against the novels themselves. Her final appeal joins the practical conditions of writing to continued experiment in subjects, sentences and forms.

sections.heading: The three parts and the flat’s doors
paragraphs: Kafka divides the novella into three parts. The first concentrates on the morning Gregor cannot leave for work and the effort to open his locked bedroom door. The second follows the family’s accommodation to his condition, including the disputed removal of furniture. The third introduces the lodgers and develops the household’s final decision about his continued presence.

The flat’s arrangement gives these changes a visible structure. Gregor hears conversations through doors, hides before other people enter and attempts to judge events from his restricted position. The room that initially contains his work and personal possessions gradually becomes a place where unwanted objects are stored. Changes to this small space record decisions about whether he is still to be treated as a member of the family.

sections.heading: What Gregor can understand and communicate
paragraphs: The narrative remains close to Gregor’s thoughts even after his speech becomes unintelligible to the people outside his room. He considers train times, excuses to his employer and his family’s needs while his listeners respond to the altered sound of his voice. Readers therefore retain access to intentions that the other characters increasingly refuse or fail to recognise.

His preferences also change in ways he struggles to assess. Fresh food that he once liked becomes unappealing, while scraps offered by Grete suit him better. Crawling on the walls gives him new activity, yet removing the furniture threatens his connection with his former life. Kafka records these incompatible responses without supplying an explanation for the original transformation. The change is established at the start and never resolved by a medical diagnosis or an account of how it occurred.

sections.heading: Grete’s music and the family’s calculations
paragraphs: Before the transformation, Gregor intends to pay for Grete to attend the conservatory. Her violin playing later draws him out towards the lodgers, whose initial interest gives way to dissatisfaction. Gregor’s response to the music recalls an ambition for his sister that she has not fully known. The episode places his continuing attachment beside the household’s increasingly commercial use of its rooms.

The family finances contain information Gregor had not understood while he was earning. His father has retained some money, and the other members gradually obtain employment. This does not make their altered circumstances comfortable, but it complicates Gregor’s conviction that all survival depends on him. The closing movement follows the parents and Grete outside the flat, after the narrative has spent most of its time within or immediately around Gregor’s room.

sections.heading: The two later prefatory documents
paragraphs: Brontë’s Preface to the second edition is dated 21 December 1847 and signed Currer Bell. It thanks readers and reviewers, answers objections about the novel’s religious tendency and dedicates the new edition to William Makepeace Thackeray. These are responses to the reception of an already published book; the first edition had no corresponding Preface.

The Note to the Third Edition, dated 13 April 1848, has a more specific purpose. Currer Bell states that the claim to be a novelist rests on Jane Eyre alone and corrects the attribution of other works of fiction to the same author. Read beside the use of pseudonyms by the Brontë sisters, the document records a practical problem of literary identification, rather than a revision to Jane’s story.

sections.heading: Teaching as paid work
paragraphs: Jane spends eight years at Lowood, six as a pupil and two as a teacher. She obtains the Thornfield post by placing an advertisement and corresponding about a position teaching a child under fourteen. Mrs Fairfax offers a salary of thirty pounds a year. The employment is negotiated before Jane knows Rochester or understands the household into which she is entering.

Her later work at the village school near Moor House provides a different teaching situation. She begins with limited expectations of the pupils but comes to recognise their individual abilities and progress. Comparing the two posts keeps Jane’s independence connected to a skill she can exchange for income. An inheritance changes her financial position later; it does not erase the years in which she supports herself by teaching.

sections.heading: Reading, drawing and the adult narrator
paragraphs: The first chapter introduces Jane as a reader looking at Bewick’s History of British Birds behind a window curtain. Books recur as possessions, sources of images and occasions for judgement. Her drawings also become evidence of an inner life that others do not immediately understand: Rochester examines her portfolio and questions her about its unusual subjects.

The story is presented as the autobiography of an adult recounting her earlier life. Jane can reproduce a child’s fear while also explaining circumstances that the child could not then assess. Her direct addresses to the reader make the act of telling visible. The final chapter explicitly locates the account ten years into her marriage, giving readers a point from which to understand the distance between narrated experience and retrospective statement.

sections.heading: Different claims made in the name of religion
paragraphs: Brocklehurst, Helen Burns, Miss Temple and St John Rivers do not represent a single religious position. Brocklehurst enforces deprivation on the pupils while his own family enjoys luxury; Helen advises endurance and forgiveness; Miss Temple investigates Jane’s treatment and offers practical care. St John later asks Jane to adopt missionary work as a vocation under his direction. The differences are established through conduct and conversation, allowing the novel’s religious arguments to be examined through particular relationships.

sections.heading: Earlier printings and a later rearrangement
paragraphs: The 1609 quarto was not the first appearance in print of every poem. Versions of Sonnets 138 and 144 had appeared in The Passionate Pilgrim in 1599, a miscellany whose title page attributed the whole collection to Shakespeare although it included work by other writers. The earlier versions provide evidence of textual variation before the complete sequence was printed.

John Benson’s 1640 edition presented a substantially different arrangement, regrouping poems and supplying titles. Following the 1609 order therefore preserves a specific early publication rather than an arrangement shared by every historical edition. The dedication signed by Thomas Thorpe belongs to that publication history; it does not securely identify the person behind every address within the poems.

sections.heading: The usual form and its exceptions
paragraphs: Most poems have fourteen lines in iambic pentameter, with three alternating-rhyme quatrains followed by a rhyming couplet: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. A quatrain can extend an example, qualify an assertion or introduce a new comparison. The couplet may state a conclusion, but it can also change the force of what came before. Punctuation and the movement of a sentence across line endings are therefore as useful as the rhyme scheme when following an argument.

Three conspicuous exceptions prevent this pattern from becoming an inflexible rule. Sonnet 99 has fifteen lines because its opening unit contains five. Sonnet 126 comprises twelve lines arranged as six couplets. Sonnet 145 uses four-beat lines rather than the usual five. These are features of the transmitted poems, not gaps or mistakes that an editor should automatically regularise.

sections.heading: Reading linked poems in small groups
paragraphs: Some of the most useful comparisons are between immediate neighbours. Sonnets 27 and 28 connect daytime labour with wakefulness at night. Sonnets 97, 98 and 99 return to separation through winter, April and flowers, but the season described and the speaker’s emotional account do not always coincide. The sequence supplies repeated material on which to test changes of emphasis.

Other poems place pressure on familiar conventions of praise. Sonnet 130 lists comparisons the speaker declines to make about his mistress, then affirms his attachment in the couplet. Sonnet 138 describes a relationship sustained by statements both parties know are unreliable. These poems are useful alongside more frequently quoted declarations because the collection includes scepticism, embarrassment, negotiation and self-accusation as well as claims of constancy. The labels used for groups of sonnets are aids to reading, not a substitute for the wording of each poem.

sections.heading: A route through the twenty-four books
paragraphs: After the opening quarrel, Books II–VII establish the opposing forces and several leading fighters. They include the catalogue of ships, the proposed duel between Menelaus and Paris, Diomed’s fighting and Hector’s return to Troy. Book IX sends an embassy to Achilles with an offer of gifts, but persuasion fails to bring him back into battle. The fighting subsequently moves towards the Greek ships.

Patroclus enters combat in Book XVI. His death leads to the struggle over his body, Achilles’ decision to return and the making of new armour. Hector dies in Book XXII, but two substantial books remain: the funeral games for Patroclus and Priam’s visit to recover his son. The poem’s structure gives negotiation, burial and the organisation of remembrance space after the principal duel.

sections.heading: Names in Butler’s translation
paragraphs: Butler’s naming conventions can initially obscure connections with other translations. Jove is Zeus, Juno is Hera, Minerva is Athena, Neptune is Poseidon, Mars is Ares, Venus is Aphrodite and Vulcan is Hephaestus. Ulysses corresponds to Odysseus, while Butler commonly writes Diomed for Diomedes and Alexandrus for Paris. Keeping these equivalents in view avoids mistaking alternative names for additional characters.

The Greeks themselves are collectively called Achaeans, Argives and Danaans at different points. These terms usually refer to the same expeditionary force rather than three armies with separate objectives. References to a man as the son of Atreus or the son of Peleus likewise require attention to family: Agamemnon and Menelaus are both sons of Atreus, while Achilles is the son of Peleus. Context establishes which person is meant.

sections.heading: Encounters beyond single combat
paragraphs: In Book VI, Glaucus and Diomed discover a bond of hospitality between their families and exchange armour instead of fighting. Later in the same book, Hector meets Andromache and their child inside Troy. These scenes introduce obligations and relationships that extend beyond a warrior’s immediate performance on the battlefield.

The shield made for Achilles in Book XVIII contains cities, a dispute before elders, agricultural work, a vineyard, herds and dancing. It places scenes of civilian activity on an object intended for combat. Book XXIII similarly broadens the action through athletic contests, prizes, disagreements and settlements at Patroclus’s funeral. Reading these episodes alongside the battle books makes clear how much of the epic concerns speech, exchange, work and social order. Butler renders all of these passages in prose, so readers can follow their narrative sequence while using the notes for names and unfamiliar practices.

sources.label: Homer: The Iliad in Samuel Butler’s translation
